procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 13.08.2013 passed by the Sub-Divisional Judicial Magistrate, Patna, rejecting the application filed under Section 205 Cr.P.C. (Code of Criminal Procedure) for exemption from personal appearance.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The accused-appellants challenged the Magistrate's order by filing an application under Section 482 Cr.P.C. before the Patna High Court. The High Court dismissed the application on 17.04.2017, taking a new ground that a prayer for exemption from personal appearance under Section 205 Cr.P.C. can only be made at the stage of first appearance of the accused.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The accused-appellants, aggrieved by the Patna High Court's order dated 17.04.2017, filed a Criminal Appeal (No. 387 of 2018) before the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the orders of both the High Court and the Magistrate, and allowed the application filed by the appellants under Section 205 Cr.P.C., exempting them from personal appearance.

issue.issue_text: Whether an application for exemption from personal appearance under Section 205 Cr.P.C. can be rejected on the ground that it was filed at a subsequent stage after the accused had appeared before the court.

facts: The High Court rejected an application for exemption from personal appearance under Section 205 Cr.P.C.
The High Court's reasoning was that such an application can only be made at the first appearance of the accused, and not at a subsequent stage after the accused has already appeared in person.
The Supreme Court found that the accused had actually filed the application on 17.01.2013, which was *prior* to their appearance in court.
law: Section 205 Cr.P.C. allows a Magistrate to dispense with the personal attendance of an accused.
Section 317 Cr.P.C. empowers a Magistrate to exempt an accused from personal appearance at any stage of an inquiry or trial.
application: The Supreme Court first determined that the High Court's primary reason for rejection was factually incorrect. The application was filed before the accused appeared, not after.
The Court noted that the original Magistrate had not rejected the application on the ground that it was filed too late; this was a new and incorrect ground introduced by the High Court.

The Supreme Court also addressed the High Court's observation that the accused should have used Section 317 Cr.P.C. It pointed out that Section 317 also gives the Magistrate the power to grant exemption at any stage.
This confirmed that there was no procedural bar or lack of power preventing the Magistrate from considering the application for exemption, regardless of the stage.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's reasoning, holding that its basis for dismissal was "unfounded" and factually incorrect. The Court concluded that there was no impediment to the Magistrate considering the application for exemption, as it was filed before the accused's appearance, and in any event, the court has the power to grant such an exemption at any stage of the proceedings.

issue.issue_text: Whether an application for exemption from personal appearance under Section 205 Cr.P.C. can be rejected on the ground that the petitioners are hale and hearty and not suffering from any disease that would prevent them from appearing in court.

facts: Petitioners filed an application under Section 205 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.) seeking exemption from personal appearance in court.

One of the primary reasons given by the Magistrate for the rejection was that the petitioners appeared to be 'hale and hearty' and were not suffering from any disease that would be an impediment to appearing in court.
law: A court must consider the actual grounds presented in an application and provide relevant reasons for its decision. A reason that does not address the applicant's claims is not a valid basis for rejection.
application: The Supreme Court found the Magistrate's reason that the petitioners were 'hale and hearty' to be 'wholly out of place'.
The Court noted that the petitioners had not filed their application on the grounds of physical illness. Therefore, their physical health was irrelevant to the request.
The actual grounds for the exemption request were the significant distance (1750 kms) between their residence in Pune and the court in Patna, as well as their professional and student commitments.

The Supreme Court held that the Magistrate committed an error by failing to consider the actual grounds presented by the petitioners and instead rejecting the application for an unfounded and irrelevant reason.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the Magistrate's reasoning, holding that an application for exemption from personal appearance cannot be denied on the grounds that the petitioners are 'hale and hearty' when their application was not based on a claim of physical illness. This reason was deemed irrelevant and 'wholly out of place'.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an application for exemption from personal appearance under Section 205 Cr.P.C. can be rejected on the ground that it was filed at a subsequent stage after the accused had appeared before the court.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the High Court's observation that the application under Section 205 Cr.P.C. was filed at a subsequent stage after appearing before the court was factually incorrect.
respondent_arguments: The respondent likely defended the High Court's decision, arguing that the application was correctly rejected because it was filed at a later stage after the accused had already appeared.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an application for exemption from personal appearance under Section 205 Cr.P.C. can be rejected on the ground that the petitioners are hale and hearty and not suffering from any disease that would prevent them from appearing in court.
appellant_arguments: The appellant implicitly argued that being 'hale and hearty' is not a valid ground for rejecting an application for exemption from personal appearance, as the provision is not limited to cases of illness.
respondent_arguments: The respondent likely supported the lower court's reasoning that since the accused were not suffering from any disease, there was no valid reason to grant them an exemption from personal appearance.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An application for exemption from personal appearance under Section 205 of the Criminal Procedure Code cannot be rejected on the ground that the nature of the offence requires the accused to be present on each and every date.
obiter: The observation of the High Court that the accused has filed application under Section 205 Cr.P.C. at a subsequent stage after appearing before the court is factually incorrect.
The High Court took entirely new grounds for dismissing the application filed under Section 482 Cr.P.C. without adverting to the grounds which were taken by the Magistrate for declining the prayer.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that the rejection of the application for exemption from personal appearance under Section 205 Cr.P.C. was based on entirely invalid grounds. The Magistrate's reason that the accused were 'hale and hearty' was deemed 'wholly out of place' because the application was not made on grounds of illness. Furthermore, the High Court's reason for rejection—that the application was filed after the accused had already appeared—was found to be factually incorrect, as the application was filed prior to their appearance, rendering that ground 'unfounded'.
policy_considerations: The court rejected the idea that an accused's personal presence can be mandated simply in the hope that 'good sense' will prevail between the parties or to facilitate conciliation, stating: 'We fail to see this as any valid ground for not considering actual grounds given by the accused for seeking exemption.'
